reason: The sources provide enough supported claims to form a 45-second script about the platypus's discovery hoax and biology.
story: In 1799, British naturalists received a bizarre specimen from Australia featuring a duck's bill, a beaver-like tail, and furry mammalian skin. Convinced it was an elaborate hoax stitched together by Asian artisans, scientist George Shaw took a pair of scissors to the pelt searching for hidden stitches. Finding none, he reluctantly named it Platypus anatinus. It took decades of debate to confirm this creature was entirely real. As science unlocked its secrets, the platypus proved even stranger than a fake. It is a venomous mammal that lays leathery eggs, hunts entirely blind underwater using electrosorption to detect prey, and remarkably, glows a vibrant cyan and green under ultraviolet light.
angle: The first scientists to examine a platypus thought it was a fake animal sewn together from spare parts.

claims.claim: In 1799, the first scientists to examine a preserved platypus body judged it a fake made of several animals sewn together.
George Shaw produced the first description of the animal in the Naturalist's Miscellany in 1799.
George Shaw used a pair of scissors to check the specimen for stitches.
Robert Knox believed the specimen might have been created by Chinese sailors.
The male platypus has a spur on each hind foot that delivers an extremely painful venom.
The platypus is one of the five extant species of monotremes, mammals that lay eggs instead of giving birth to live young.
The platypus relies on electrolocation when feeding, as the eyes, ears, and nose are closed while underwater.
William Hay Caldwell confirmed in 1884 that the female platypus lays eggs.
Captain John Hunter, the second Governor of New South Wales, sent a pelt and sketch back to Great Britain in 1798.

disputed: Whether Robert Knox or other naturalists suspected Chinese sailors specifically because of trade routes through the Indian Ocean; script should attribute this: according to one account, naturalists suspected Chinese sailors known for stitching hybrid creatures.
